messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Captain Linh

Linh was twenty-three when she took the helm of a container vessel—the youngest captain in her company's history, a distinction that had once filled her with pride. Her childhood in a cramped apartment in San Jose with her father had been something else entirely. He had been a man of sudden rages, his hand quick and his voice quicker, and by the time she was old enough to understand that other children did not flinch at raised voices, the damage was already woven into her nervous system. Her father had favored the dark—he would wait for her in unlit hallways, would pull her into shadowed rooms to punish her for small infractions, real or imagined. The physical blows came with unpredictable force, and the darkness had become inseparable from the terror. Now, at twenty-three, Linh commanded a crew of forty men across open water, yet she was imprisoned by the very conditions that had shaped her earliest fears.

Nighttime had become unbearable. When Linh woke in the darkness of her captain's quarters, her body would flood with adrenaline before her conscious mind had even registered where she was. The darkness itself—the simple absence of light—triggered an immediate cascade: her muscles would tense, her breathing would shallow, her mind would race through scenarios of danger that had no rational foothold in her present reality. She had come to believe that darkness was inherently unsafe, that it was a condition in which bad things happened to her, and this conviction meant that every evening as the sun descended, her body began its familiar countdown to threat. She would lie rigid in her bunk, waiting for sleep that would not come, her hand always positioned near the light switch. The darkness was not merely uncomfortable; it was a return to a state of helplessness that her adult self could not tolerate.

What frightened her most was being alone with men. The presence of a man in an enclosed space—her first officer in the chart room, a crew member needing repairs in her quarters—triggered the same bodily response as the darkness. Her muscles would coil, her senses would sharpen to an almost painful degree, and she would find herself automatically scanning for exits, mentally mapping the distance to the door, calculating whether she could move past him if she needed to. This hypervigilance had become so automatic that she barely noticed it anymore; it was simply how her body responded to male presence. She was certain that men were fundamentally dangerous, that proximity to them meant vulnerability, and this conviction meant that every interaction with her crew carried an undercurrent of threat that exhausted her. When she had to drive her truck to the port with one of her officers—a routine part of her job—her hands would grip the steering wheel so tightly that her knuckles would blanch, and she would feel her body bracing for violence that never came.

The nighttime and the isolation had begun to feed each other in ways that had quietly reshaped her life. She avoided driving with crew members whenever possible, citing scheduling conflicts or preferring to travel alone, which had earned her a reputation for aloofness. She had stopped attending evening crew gatherings, the informal social events that bound a ship's complement together, because they occurred after dark and often involved male colleagues in close quarters. Her isolation had deepened her conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with her—that normal people did not live in this state of constant readiness, did not view the world as a minefield of danger, did not find themselves cut off from the very people who depended on her leadership. The more she withdrew, the more isolated she felt, and the more isolated she felt, the more convinced she became that she was defective in some essential way. She began to wonder if her crew could sense her fear, if they knew that their captain was not truly in control, and this shame only deepened her resolve to keep everyone at a distance.

Linh had finally sought help after a crew member found her having a panic attack in the engine room at 0300 hours. She had woken from a nightmare in complete darkness, disoriented, and had fled her quarters in a state of terror. What brought her through the therapist's door was not hope but desperation—the recognition that the very strategies that had once protected her were now destroying her ability to do the job she had worked so hard to earn, and the growing certainty that she would never be free of the person her father had taught her to fear.
